utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. There is case number IT-03-68, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, ladies and gentlemen, good morning. I fully understand the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Oric. You may sit down and good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, leads counsel for the Prosecution, and also good morning to the Defence. I'm here together with co-counsel Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio and our case manager, Mrs. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Mr. Oric?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours and my learned friends. My name is Vasvija Vidovic and together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. With us are our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Radojicic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As you may have noticed already what I am saying in English and what others will be saying in English for that matter will be translated to you in our own language by our interpreters. I would like to make it clear to you that interpretation is extremely necessary because we need to follow what you say and you need to follow what we are saying, that if at any time it is faulty or you're not receiving it, please draw our attention to it straight away so that we will address the matter. You are soon going to start giving evidence as a witness for the Prosecution. Our rules require that before you do so, you make a solemn declaration to the effect that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text is contained in a piece of paper which you are just being handed now. Please read it out loud and that will be your solemn declaration undertaking with us. It is equivalent to an oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please do sit down. Let me introduce myself, first of all. I'm the Presiding Judge and my name is Carmel Agius. I come from Malta. To my right I have Judge Hans Hendrik Brydensholt from the Kingdom of Denmark and to my left I have Judge Albin Eser from Germany. Together we are presiding over this case which the Prosecution has instituted against Naser Oric. You will first be asked a series of questions by Mr. Di Fazio whom I'm sure you have already met, and he will then be followed by Mr. Jones who is co-counsel assisting Madam Vidovic in the defence of Mr. Oric. My recommendation to you is that in answering your questions, apart from being truthful in your answer and as precise as possible, I would like you to be as concise as possible as well. So don't try to give us more information than you are being asked for and if a question can be answered by a simple yes or no, then answer it by a simple yes or no. In other words, please try to answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, you may begin. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, just for the purposes of the Defence I think I'm going to be fairly brief this morning so I'll definitely get a start obviously today but it's possible I could finish before the break. I'll be fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You are prepared for that, I suppose, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you both.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Radojicic I just want to run some personal details past you and I want you to tell us if they are correct or not. You were born on the 24th of September 1955, you're of Serb ethnicity, you're married, you have three children, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You graduated from the faculty of law in Mostar in 1974, you started your JNA training in December of 1979 and finished it in October 1980; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In July of 1982 you started to work in the - I'm not sure of the pronunciation - Nevesinje -- Nevesinje municipality where you were the secretary for economic affairs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You did that for four years and then in 1986 you became secretary for the municipal assembly and you held that position for another four years, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: August of 1990 you became the head of the municipal board, a position that you kept for about four months and in January 1991, you became the TO commander for the Nevesinje municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In March of 1992, you joined the JNA as a captain and thereafter remained in the army, later in its incarnation as the VRS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In May of 1992, to August of 1994, you were deputy commander of the 3rd infantry battalion of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: The 3rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. From August of 1994 to November of 1995 you became commander of the 3rd Infantry Battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And those two last positions that I just described to you were -- were those battalions, the 3rd Infantry Battalion, were they part of the 8th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In February of 1995 you were promoted to captain first class and you moved to 708 Brigade headquarters -- and you moved to the 708 Brigade headquarters in November of 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You were a reservist essentially until June of 1996 whereupon you became a professional member of the VRS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You were promoted to major in January of 1995 and you continued to remain at 708 Brigade headquarters until February of 1997, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: February of 1997 you became deputy commander of personnel in 708 Brigade and you remained in that position until March of 2002 and in June of that -- of 2000, you were promoted to Lieutenant Colonel. Are those details correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I think I have this right. During the period of time that you were deputy commander of personnel at 708 Brigade, you became head of department of operations and education, and also you were appointed deputy commander of 708 Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: This was as of the 1st of March 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks. From September 2003 to June of 2004, you were commander of the 708 Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And from June of last year, 2004, you have been the head of Department for Civil and Military Cooperation of the 5th Reserve Division of the VRS based at Sokolac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In late 2004, as a result of a request for assistance from the Office of the Prosecutor, did you receive an order requiring you to examine certain documents and collate information relating to certain documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you subsequently make inquiries of fellow officers, including retired officers, and examine -- let me withdraw that and start the question again. Did you subsequently make inquiries of fellow officers, including retired officers, regarding a collection of documents held by the 5th Reserve Division?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, especially after I learned I would appear as a witness before the Tribunal in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And also, as a result of that, did you actually come to examine certain documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I didn't examine the documents because in November 2004 the documents were transferred to the Ministry of Defence in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. But did you see the documents and locate the documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I saw the documents in late November 2004 pursuant to a document issued by the General Staff of the army of Republika Srpska about the sending of a report on these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And did that -- thank you. Did the order that you've spoken of asking you to look into the background and history of documentation carry with it an annex listing certain specific documents, 186 them in all?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: That order contained a list of the documents about which a report was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like you to look at this particular list. It's not in dispute, Mr. Radojicic, that this list that you have had just produced to you was in fact attached to the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, is that so?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. And I think your list will show that you signed the back of -- the back of it on the 24th of March 2005; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And if you go to the end of the list, you'll see that it relates to 186 documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please I seek to tender that list into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. What is the next number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document will become Prosecution Exhibit P546. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I have also prepared or caused to be prepared a further list which is based on this list. It's not a list that this witness has prepared himself but one that's been produced by the Prosecution and it's based entirely on this. It's got 186 documents. It's in English. I have added to it a column which contains the corresponding list of Prosecution exhibits. So it's more of a tool, a reference tool, and I'd like to tender that into evidence but I don't know what the attitude of the -- of the Defence is to that and it's so that you can follow the evidence more clearly and will be useful perhaps one day when you want to come to compare the particular documents with the actual exhibits in our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine so. It's indeed a very helpful document, this, which I have had the opportunity to see the like of in other cases. So although I would have reserved our position until I heard Mr. Jones, I would have anticipated also what the Defence reaction would be. Yes, this will become P547 and I thank you for it, Mr. Di Fazio, please. Yes, next. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, we will get to the issue of the documents that you actually looked at in late 2004. Let me rephrase that. As a result of receiving the order from the -- your superiors to look into the question of documentation, including these 186 documents, did you speak to your superior, a gentleman named Colonel Nedjo Gavric?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And about when was that? When did you speak with him about documentation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Just after I received the order from my superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what did Colonel Nedjo Gavric tell you regarding documentation in the possession of the 5th Reserve Division?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Colonel Gavric told me that in June 2004, he had received these documents from the staff commander and that he had handed them on to the commander of the division.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did he provide you with any information as to the more distant history of the documents -- of this collection of documents, where they were originally found?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: He told me that these documents which had been delivered to him were documents seized during the operation in July 1995 in Srebrenica. He didn't give me any other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he tell you where you might locate these documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: He told me that the documents were with the deputy division commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And who was the deputy division commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: The deputy division commander was Colonel Ranko Prodanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And where -- where were you physically located when -- where is Prodanovic's office actually located, what town, village, where? Where is it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: The command of the 5th Division is located in Sokolac. That's where these offices are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And about how far out of Sarajevo is Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Approximately 43 or 44 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time you had this conversation with Gavric, did you have that list, Exhibit P546, the -- the -- your list of 186 documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: At the time of my conversation with Colonel Gavric I didn't have these documents, until we went to the office of the deputy commander of the 5th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Sure, but did you actually have the list -- the list of -- setting out the documents that the Office of the Prosecutor was interested in? Did you have that list of documents when you spoke to Gavric?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did have the list, because it had been attached to the order I had received.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. So you've got the list. You've spoken to Gavric. And you've told us that you went to see Prodanovic in his office. What happened when you went and saw Mr. -- I'm sorry, I've forgotten his rank, Mr. Prodanovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I told Colonel Prodanovic about the document we had received, and he told me that he had these documents in his office in the safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did he open the safe and produce anything?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: He opened the safe and took out two folders of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at this point, you had the -- your list and he had these two folders of documents. Did you actually compare the listed 186 documents in the -- in the annex that you've already -- that you've told us about that you had in your possession with documents in the two folders? Did you compare all of them, some of them, or none of them?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I compared about 20 documents, not in sequence. It was in random.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did you conclude that the folders contained -- well, let me rephrase that. Having compared about 20 of the documents with the list of documents in the annex, what did you then do?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: When I compared the 20 documents, I saw that these were originals to be found on the list that was annexed to the order, and I spoke with Colonel Prodanovic so as to see what would be the further procedure concerning the chain of custody of the documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And can you tell us or can you not tell us which 20 in particular you compared on the list with the -- with the 20 in the -- in the two folders?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell the Trial Chamber if the two folders contained a lot more than 186 -- than the 186 documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: There were more documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. What did you and Prodanovic decide to do about this -- these two folders of documents and this request for information regarding the 186 documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: We discussed it and we concluded that the best solution should be that that documentation be turned over to the security organ and forwarded to the Ministry of Defence in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And how did you physically achieve this? And I'd like you to tell us the names of persons who were involved in the process of transferring the documents out of the safe of Prodanovic to Banja Luka. How did you go about this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Colonel Prodanovic invited Lieutenant Colonel Sakota Kosta, who was the head of security in Sokolac, and we showed him the documents. He said that he agrees with our decision to transfer the documentation to Banja Luka so that it would be closer to the government and its department for cooperation with The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I may not have asked you this but when you first saw the documents in Prodanovic's office, where were they located? In his desk, in a cupboard? Where precisely?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I think I replied to that question earlier. They were in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Thanks. All right. So Lieutenant Colonel Kosta Sakota agreed that the documents should be transferred. Did anything happen to the documents at that point?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Immediately after taking over the documents from the office of the deputy commander, Lieutenant Colonel Sakota left to Banja Luka and handed over the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So he took -- he took possession of the two folders of documents and left with them and that was the last you saw of them, I take it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry, you tell us precisely what happened.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: As I said, the documents were transferred to Banja Luka and given to the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And Kosta Sakota took the documents from you and Prodanovic and took them off to Banja Luka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And when you say the documents, do you mean the two bundles or folders of documents that Prodanovic had produced from his safe?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, that happened, I believe, in late or late November 2004, correct -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, it's not in dispute that in March of this year you provided a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. At the time that you provided the statement to the investigator, Mr. Nasir, did he ask you to make further inquiries about the provenance and custody of the documents which had been found in the two folders in Prodanovic's safe?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nasir, after I gave the statement in the office of the Hague Tribunal in Sarajevo, asked me should I appear as a witness in this proceeding before the Tribunal and should I acquire additional information about the chain of custody that I say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you in fact make some inquiries?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did you speak to anyone?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I did, in particular with a retired major of the VRS, Mr. Pejic Cedomir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. During that meeting with Mr. Pejic, Major Pejic, did you -- did you make notes of your conversation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened during the -- what was said during the conversation, what Pejic told you, without referring to your notes or do you need them to be able to recall what he told you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I don't need the notes. I can recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thanks. Okay, well, can you tell us, please, what Major Pejic told you about the documents? And in particular, can you tell him -- can you tell the Trial Chamber how it was that you and Pejic knew that you were both talk -- that were you both talking about the same set of documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Since I met Mr. Pejic when I came to Sokolac and we became friends, I asked him in relation to the colleagues who worked with me in Sokolac, who suggested to me that I could learn more about the documentation from Mr. Pejic, hence when I explained to him what it was about, he gave me the following information. At the end of 1995, Mr. Pejic was appointed as battalion commander within the Milici Brigade. In the premises of his battalion, there was also the documentation seized in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can I just ask you to pause there? Do you -- in your conversation with Major Pejic, did he ever tell you where the premises of his battalion was or do you have your own knowledge, or your own independent knowledge, where the premises of his battalion was?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I don't know that and I didn't insist on learning that piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Please continue with what Major Pejic told you.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: After that, at the beginning of 1996, Major Stanisic and Lieutenant Terzic, who was a security officer, came to see Major Pejic. They separated those documents and transferred it to Sekovici. After the 5th Corps was formed on the 31st of January 1997, that documentation was transferred from Sekovici to Sokolac. The person who was tasked with dealing with the documentation was Major Ranko Todorovic who worked on or in intelligence. By the end of 2000, the corps command received an order pertaining to collecting the documentation on the crimes committed over the Serbian people and the order regulated that the documentation be presented to The Hague Tribunal investigators. This was done and around mid-2001. Concerning the annex that is the list of documents that went together with the order from 2004, it is clear that Mr. Todorovic surrendered those documents to the investigators for scanning. After Mr. Todorovic left the 5th Corps command, the person in charge of the documentation was Major Pejic, with whom I spoke earlier. He was tasked with garrison affairs. This was in February 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Around the middle of 2003, the 5th Corps command of the VRS, with a view of the changes that happened then, issued an order setting up the new commission that was tasked with collecting and having custody over the documentation about crimes against the Serbian people, and the person responsible was Colonel Mihajlo Vujovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was he also responsible for looking after and keeping in -- the custody of the documents in the two folders that were in Prodanovic's safe?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And were the other persons you have mentioned also responsible for keeping custody of the two folders of documents in the safe of Mr. Prodanovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just give me a moment, because I think I may have finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As much as you like, or as you require, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour, I can start but since we didn't anticipate starting before the first break even --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want a break now, no, it's -- we can accommodate -- I can understand that, having been on that side for the large part of my career.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's also that we don't actually have physical copies of our exhibits here with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have the break now and then we'll resume. I'll -- do you think you will finish today?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have -- we can also have a 30-minute break, all right? Which will give you ample opportunity to organise yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's helpful. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. --- Break taken at 9.50 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry for the delay but in the meantime we had a long meeting, the three judges, on matters related to the case and we'll possibly be coming back to you for another meeting in my Chamber in the course of either later on this week or next week to discuss a few matters but everything seems to be going on well from the organisational point of view. So let's start. Are you -- did you have enough time, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So he is in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Radojicic, you spent more than ten years in the JNA and then the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You spent more than ten years in the army, correct, in various positions in the JNA and then subsequently in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the JNA I was a reserve officer from March 1992 and I have become a professional soldier with the VRS as of the 1st of July 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Precisely. So since 1992, so more than ten years, and you've occupied a number of positions of authority, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in that capacity, you've dealt with documents and archives to a great extent, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Partially so. After the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to start by outlining for you a system of keeping documents and then ask you some questions about it. Now, in the system, this is a general tell which I'm describing firstly and we'll come to details in a moment, but in the system which I'm going to ask you to imagine, when documents are seized firstly there is a written protocol or minutes to that effect, that then those documents are either numbered sequentially in the way that we see with ERN numbers used at the ICTY, sequence of numbers, or entered in a log and then archived with other documents and only transferred with some written minutes by an archivist. Do you understand the system which I've just described to you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you agree that that's a proper system of archiving documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that system is well known in the JNA and in the VRS, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance I would like to pass up an exhibit. The ERN number is 01330469. Just while that's being passed up for the record it's a document of the command of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade and it's dated 4th of March 1995. I'll ask to you look at this, Mr. Radojicic, and I'm going to draw your attention in particular to paragraphs 1 and 3. This is an order coming from the command of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade that first of all archived material for 1992 and 1993 should be collected, sorted, and submitted to the office head. In particular I'd like to draw your attention to paragraph 3 which sets out the responsibility -- which sets out what those responsible for documents must do and it states there that the documents are to be arranged chronologically, that those responsible must indicate on each document how long it is to be kept, that the items required for further use in the service shall remain with the user whilst required that those responsible should sign a receipt for these items from the office head. Then it goes on to describe various protocols which have to record various items of documentation. Now, my question is firstly: This is a document of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. Would you agree that they don't have their own unique system of archiving, this is simply good practice as recognised by the JNA and then the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't it right that the history of the documents which we have been discussing this morning and which you've been testifying about, the history of record keeping as regards those documents doesn't come close, don't even remotely resemble such a proper system of document archiving?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I could partially agree based on the statement and the knowledge I have, that documentation was most of the time with the security organ and they had their own separate system of both keeping and archiving, and I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: First actually before we go on, can I is ask for an exhibit number, please, for that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will become Defence Exhibit D--

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 286, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 286, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Taking this one step at a time with regard to the -- the documents you've testified about, firstly, it's right isn't it that everything you've told us that you've learnt about the history of these documents was told to you orally? There is no written record or protocol which you've produced?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Firstly, there is no written record, is there, of the seizure of these documents allegedly in Srebrenica from July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then these documents have been passed from person to person. I've counted at least six transactions, and correct me if I'm wrong about this, but from a Mr. Pejic to Mr. Stanisic, and Terzic to Todorovic, copy to the ICTY, back to Pejic, to Mihajlo Vujovic, to Colonel Ranko Prodanovic, at least six transactions and in none of those transactions is there any record of these documents being passed from one person to the next.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: There is the record pertaining to the handing over of the documents to Colonel Sakota.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. That's the very last link in the chain, but for the prior six links, there is no written record whatsoever, is there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: We didn't receive such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the record pertaining to the handing over of the documents to Colonel Sakota, that dates from November 2004, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: At no stage were these documents sequentially numbered, were they? By you, by the VRS, or the security organs?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Nor are you familiar, are you, with any logbook in which these documents were entered by the VRS or by the security organs?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And isn't it right that as a result of all that, a document could be slipped in among the bundle without being detected? Or a document could be removed from these folders you've described without detection precisely because there is no protocol, there is no logbook, which would show that that had happened?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: There is such a possibility if a system hasn't been set up the way it should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in this case, the system hasn't been set up as it should have done with regard to these documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: From what we can see, it was that the system was not set up as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I don't know if you can help us with this but presumably the VRS has archives of tens of thousands of documents, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: There is probably even more, but lately what has been carried out was the resorting and rearranging of the entire archival material of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And those tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands, however many documents there are, they are kept in proper archives, aren't they? They are not kept in safes of military officers?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, do you have any idea why these particular documents that you've been testifying about have been singled out for special treatment? In other words, have not been properly archived?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You don't know why they were -- when you first came across these documents, why they were being kept in the safe of a -- MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, the question assumes special treatment. It's certainly that the -- the witness has certainly said that there is a system of archiving and that these are -- have not -- these documents have obviously been held outside of that system but also assumes that that was done deliberately and it's been the receipt of some special treatment, the documents have been the receipt of some special treatment. If this witness knows that they have been specially taken aside and placed in the safe, then so be it, I've got no objection to the question. The problem is the assumption is already there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. The question in the end was rephrased to why they weren't properly archived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm happy to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I would, exactly. Please proceed along those lines, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: First, in your experience of dealing with documents held by the VRS, have you come across any other documents kept in the safes of officers rather than in the archives proper?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Well, these documents that were seized in Srebrenica also contained certain documents of interviews with prisoners of Bosniak ethnicity who had perpetrated crimes against Serbs, indictments and evidence against them was there, and this referred to Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, that's not quite the question I was asking. Let me approach it this way. You don't know, do you, why these documents were being kept in the safe of Colonel Prodanovic rather than in the archives, do you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: You are right. I assume it was for safekeeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you don't know either, do you, why there is no written chain of custody record from the seizure of these documents until you saw them, why they appear in no logbook, and why they haven't been given a protocol number?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll make a suggestion as to why none of those things were done which is that these documents are not proper documents at all and that the people, at least some of them who had custody of them, knew that, and that's why they are kept apart because they are thoroughly shady. That's my suggestion and, if you can respond to that, please do.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I would like to hear a specific question, if there is any specific doubt about the way these particular documents were kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. We can proceed to a specific example.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown D155, please? And for the -- for the record, this is in B/C/S but Prosecution did produce an English translation which I believe is P486.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the annotation that I have, filed on 3rd of February of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If the witness could also be shown P546 which is the chart which we saw from this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll start -- actually he doesn't have P546 yet, does he? Now, -- MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, may I just briefly interrupt my learned friend? Is D155 -- perhaps Mr. Jones can assist me. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Is D155 -- is that also mirrored in P65 or P68? I wonder if my friend Mr. Jones knows that from the top of his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. What I'd -- MR. DI FAZIO: Because if it is, then we are not permitted to refer to them. Or the Prosecution isn't, in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps we should move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session. I am not in a position to help you because I don't know myself. MR. DI FAZIO: I think the matter should be checked before we proceed any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think it's clear from what you've said already that in terms of the information which you obtained from Mr. Gavric, from Ranko Prodanovic, it was purely oral information, there was no written confirmation of anything they told you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was only oral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Jones, but there was some organisational matter that we had to attend to. I take it that you don't -- you're not producing another witness tomorrow, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So it's correct that what you relied on in gathering information about the history of these documents was the most basic form of record keeping, if I can put it that way, information being passed on from person to person by word of mouth?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I had to do it that way because there were no written traces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now recognition just dealing with the people you spoke to, first dealing with Colonel Ljubomir Vlacic, he didn't know anything about the chain of custody of these documents, did he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask him, but on receipt of this document, he referred me to Colonel Nedjo Gavric, to see about the documentation with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Is there -- Nedjo Gavric alive?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know of any reason why he is unable to come here and testify himself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who said that he is unable or unwilling? I think you're making an assumption there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, I'm simply saying is he unable to come here and testify, as far as the witness knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think he should answer for other people. I mean it's -- he should put that question to Mr. Di Fazio or Mr. Wubben and I don't think you will get an answer from them either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As far as information which you received from Nedjo Gavric is concerned, you weren't able to independently verify information he provided, were you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: How do you mean, independently verify?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I'll take the information step by step. First he said that the documents came from the archives of the VRS 5th Corps. You weren't able to verify that information from any other source, were you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I relied entirely on what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Precisely. Second, he said that the documents were seized during operation Krivaja, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And just for the benefit of all of us, that's the operation to seize the safe area of Srebrenica, correct, in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know if Nedjo Gavric was involved in operation Krivaja?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then thirdly, Gavric told you that the documents were kept on the premises of the 5th R Division previously called the 5th Corps of the VRS, and again for that information you rely entirely on what he told you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you at any time ask for some written confirmation or written evidence of what Gavric was telling you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As far as you know, there were no records, files, log books, nothing which would verify the comments made by Gavric?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of anything like that. I questioned our archivist and he said he had no information about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In your experience, there should be a written record, shouldn't there, of documents held by VRS?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic are you going to object to --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I only would like to have the transcript corrected. The witness said something important. He said he spoke to the archivist and that the archivist told him that they had no documentation about it, whereas here it says that they had no information about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, after giving my statement in the offices of The Hague Tribunal in Sarajevo, I asked about this and they asked whether there were any documents that had passed through the archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the clarification is so the answer that you were given related to the existence or otherwise of documents, not to the existence or otherwise of any other kind of information. You were told "we have no documents"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This refers to supporting documents, whether there were any documents. That's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear enough. Yes, let's proceed, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And just to clarify, there were none, no documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the understanding. The question is because previously the transcript used the word information rather than documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If that's clear to all of us, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I think my last question wasn't answered which was, in your experience, there should be a written record, shouldn't there, of documents held by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Certainly there should be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gavric only took over the archives on the 1st of June 2004; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So he too only first became responsible for these documents 12 years or so after they were made, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So as far as you know, he himself was relying on what other people had told him when he said these documents were seized in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, wasn't the archivist before Mr. Gavric a Vlado Lucic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Colonel Vlado Lucic was chief of the Department for Planning and Training, and the Office of General Affairs was part of his department, and there is an archivist's job provided for within that department.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. So in other words he was the responsible person before Mr. Gavric?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: That's correct. He was the responsible person. When I learned all this, I couldn't see that Vlado Lucic had any part to play in the safekeeping of these documents from what I learned later about their custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You never spoke to Vlado Lucic, did you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, once you were charged to handle this matter, you spoke to Mr. Prodanovic who had the documents in his safe, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: First I spoke to the commander, Colonel Vlacic, then to Colonel Gavric, and then the deputy commander, Colonel Prodanovic when Colonel Prodanovic told me that the documents were locked in his safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And Colonel Prodanovic had also inherited the documents from someone else, hadn't he, namely Petar Mladjenovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: At the time of the handing over between General Mladjenovic and Colonel Prodanovic, that was early June 2004. I suppose General Mladjenovic also knew of the existence of the documentation since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And again I won't pursue this point any further after this, but there was no written record of the handover from Mladjenovic to Prodanovic that you saw?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you didn't go back and speak to Mladjenovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: No. He has been retired since June 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If Your Honours would give me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to the meeting which you had with Cedomir Pejic in which you received additional information. Firstly, can you tell us the date of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: That was around the 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the information you received from him, if I'm summarising it correctly, is that towards the end of 1995, Pejic was a battalion commander within the military brigade and in the premises of the military brigade or that battalion were some of these documents. Now, firstly --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: In the very room where the battalion was set up or the battalion that Major Pejic commanded over. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So we are talk there about the end of 1995. Srebrenica of course fell in July 1995. Is it right then that there was even a gap before Pejic saw the documents, namely between July of 1995 and later in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I'd like to apologise. That was the end of 1996. I apologise for making a mistake in the earlier answer. I just wanted to make sure that this is the end of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So it's right then, isn't it, that there is a year and a half gap even between the documents allegedly being seized and Mr. Pejic coming on the scene?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then at the beginning -- your testimony was at the beginning of 1996, Mr. Stanisic and Terzic took the documents to Sekovici. Is si that still correct, the beginning of 1996?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it's just me who got the dates wrong or if it's in the transcript. But anyway, I've noted 1996. Anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have the correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's okay now. But I wouldn't know whether you got it wrong or not, Mr. Jones. Anyway, it's clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did you speak to Mr. Stanisic or Mr. Terzic about the documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: No. I did not have the opportunity. Major Stanisic passed away. I don't know the exact date. And as for Lieutenant Terzic, he is still in the active service of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Then in 1997, we have the documents going to Major Todorovic in the 5th Corps. Again, did you speak to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones, one moment. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a correction of the transcript. The witness stated that Mr. Terzic is still active with the Army of Serbia and Montenegro and not the VRS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that correction. It's important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to apologise, just a brief remark. When I said that he was a security officer, that was in 1997 when he separated those documents from the rest. That's when he was still with the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So your question, I think, do you need to repeat it, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You didn't speak to Major Todorovic about these documents either, you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: No. He is also now a member of the Serbia and Montenegro armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You said in your testimony this morning that it's clear, those were your words, that Major Todorovic released the documents to investigators. You didn't speak to him. You don't have a written minute or protocol to that effect, do you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then it appeared from your testimony that Mr. Pejic again regained custody of these documents. Don't know if you can help us with a date for when that occurred.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I believe I told you that was the end of February 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then we have in mid-2003 an order being issued for a commission regarding crimes allegedly committed against the Serb people and the person responsible was Mihajlo Vujovic. Did you speak to Mihajlo Vujovic to confirm this story?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. He is now undergoing some schooling or training.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it was never explained to you, was it, how these documents came to be in the safe of Major Prodanovic rather than in some normal archive?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: He didn't tell me that. I was told that by Colonel Gavric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that the documents seized in Srebrenica during operation Krivaja remained in the custody of the 5th Corps -- the entire time from their seizure until they were -- copies were delivered to the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: No. The 5th Corps of the VRS has been formed on the 21st of January 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me approach it a different way. It would involve a new exhibit which is -- the ERN number is 00632976 to 00632977. We have copies to hand up and it's a document from a Darko Trifunovic delivering documents to the second Prosecutor of this Tribunal, Louise Arbour. Actually my apologies, we probably don't have this in B/C/S. Let me just check. No, we do indeed. In this letter, the Law Projects Centre in Yugoslavia purports to deliver among other things, if you look at 2 A, quote, "Top secret documentation of Bosnian Muslim army captured after the fall of Srebrenica amounting to, it should probably read, 40.000 pages of written documentation." My question is, are you aware that 40.000 pages of written documentation relating to the armed forces in Srebrenica were apparently seized after the fall of Srebrenica and were then in Belgrade, at least at some point?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you find this statement in the letter of Darko Trifunovic to the effect that there are these 40.000 documents which were apparently not seized by the VRS -- well, let me rephrase that. If the documents which found their way eventually into the safe of General Prodanovic - they were seized by the VRS - do you have any explanation as to what these purported 40.000 documents refers to?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you find this statement to be credible, that there were 40.000 documents? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I object to that. This -- this witness has not offered anything that could provide a basis for his being able to comment on whether 40.000 documents were collected there or not. He's been merely telling us what others have told him and the source of the documents in the safe. He doesn't know if there were 40.000 documents collected in the town of Srebrenica or in the whole area of Srebrenica. I don't mind if he's asked that, but ask him directly and provide the basis for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're both assuming, actually, both Mr. Jones, and you, Mr. Di Fazio. I could put the question myself but I would prefer Mr. Jones did that. Just ask him for -- not to speculate, not speculation, but whether he has got any -- anything to say with regard to what is stated here that the top secret documentation captured after the fall amounted to 40.000 pages. And let's see whether he knows anything about it, whether he can comment on that, without speculating. I don't want opinions based on nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Since Your Honour has put the question rather than re-stating it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You put it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I approach it this way. Did you understand the question as phrased a moment ago by His Honour?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I did. I have no information about that. You should ask the person who wrote this letter, that Mr. Trifunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I would simply ask for an exhibit number for this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this will be D27 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: D287. Thank you. Does it have a date?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm afraid it appears to be undated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to come back briefly to this table of 186 documents. If I understand your testimony correctly, you're not able to say that each of these documents were found in Srebrenica, or if you are maintaining that, then please say so.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: If those documents were taken over by The Hague Tribunal, then I would maintain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look at some of these items then. I'd like to start by looking at P91 and if that could be shown to the witness. And it's number 105 on the spread sheet. Just for reference, this is entitled "Dossier, Serbs in the Bratunac-Srebrenica-Skelani area 1992 to 1993." And the information -- it was obtained by Deyan Mihovles from Les Amis Du Commissariat De Belgrade Pour les Refugies on 22/02/96. The original of this document appears to be in English, for a start, and it -- I would suggest -- is clearly prepared by Serbs from Bratunac because it concerns alleged crimes committed against Serbs and it describes Muslim areas as inaccessible. And that's page 500890933, it's a description of the Muslim areas being inaccessible. I'm sorry, areas that have been conquered by the Muslims have become inaccessible. Now do you seriously maintain that this document was found alongside other documents of the Bosniaks in Srebrenica when the Serbs took the enclave in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I can't say that because I didn't participate in the operation and I didn't participate in the creation of the document, and in the chain of custody until November 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So in fact it's right, isn't it, that you cannot say of each of these items that they were seized in Srebrenica in July 1995. It's not information which you possess.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I have the information based on conversations I had with people who were in charge of the documentation and I know what they told me pertaining to that. Based on those conversations I can claim that this is the documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is one thing that needs to be clarified. I don't think it can be clarified by the witness and I don't think it can be clarified by you, Mr. Jones, but it needs to be clarified in order for your question to -- and answer to be put in their proper perspective. If you look at P91, which is the document that the witness has been referred to, which is a dossier entitled "Serbs in the Bratunac/Srebrenica/Skelani area 1992-1993," which is a document in English and which is undated, and which has ERN number 00890928 to 00890935, you see as I said that this is undated. So on the face of it, since it refers to 1992 and 1993, it could or could not be in Srebrenica in 1995 when the town was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's of course possible, Your Honour. My point was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but if you look at the list that were filed -- lists that were tendered earlier on this morning, where you have reference to this document being number 105, being number 105, you see that there is there a date, commissariat, le division, 22nd February 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's when it was delivered, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. So this is what we need to have clarified. Where does this date come from? And who delivered it? And to whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And my point obviously is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And at the end of the day, if that date means that it was compiled, this report or this dossier, in 1996, obviously the conclusion is that it couldn't have been in Srebrenica in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's -- just refers to a date when the document was delivered to whoever, we would need to know who this whoever is, who delivered it and, who received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, there is that point, Your Honour, and it may be that it's the handover date but our point obviously is that it's a document prepared by the Serb side. It's in English. It was handed over in 1996 or created in 1996 and therefore we are submitting obviously not found in the files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's my point -- yes, Mr. Di Fazio, if you can enlighten us on this. MR. DI FAZIO: I can't, not -- not on the factual issue Your Honours just raised. I will have to look at that and look at the ERN and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you can. MR. DI FAZIO: But the assumption is also inherent that Mr. Jones is making is that this document was found in Srebrenica written in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which is not something which is beyond the possible. I mean -- MR. DI FAZIO: No, no it's not it's not beyond the realms of possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The original is in English. The B/C/S just for clarification, the B/C/S is a translation, the original is in English. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand that. I have no quarrel with that. Mr. Jones is perfectly correct in that. There is no problem about that. Of course, whether the English translation which was handed over by this organisation back in 1996 came from a Serbian document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the inverse. The original seems to be in English. It's the -- it's the translation that exists is from English into Serb and not the other way around. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, the translation here made in this institution here. Whether the English that was handed over by this fellow Deyan Mihovles in February 1996, he handed over the English, whether that was created from another document or translated, we simply don't know. These are matters for submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is why I said we need to clarify this. Because as it is, I can take the question and the answer. I can only take them with a pinch of salt. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand that. I'm make sure inquiries are put into place and that we try. And if we ascertain any new information regarding this, make sure that the Defence gets it immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, just to be clear, we obviously don't want to make submissions on the documents now but obviously our point goes to the likelihood of a Serb document on this subject being found in English in Srebrenica. Even if it's in B/C/S, the point remains the same, and all we have -- all we have is the English original. We don't have a B/C/S original. But I don't wish to make submissions. I would like to show a couple more examples, though, to the witness to make this point. If the witness could be shown P92, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This is 106 on the list and it's purportedly a report on destruction of houses and material goods in the Bratunac, Srebrenica, Skelani area from 1992 and 1992, and I'll just read the top it says "the above list as already mentioned is provisional and incomplete. The fact that the perpetrators of these crimes were local Muslim inhabitants renders these tragedies even greater and this is not happening for the first time in history to the Serbs in this region." And then it goes on to recount alleged destruction to Serb houses and goods. My question for you, Mr. Radojicic is: Seeing that, firstly would you agree that this is a document compiled by the Serbs of crimes allegedly committed against them?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: When I replied to this question, I will remind you that on the list of the documents that we received and that you have before you, the title actually says "documents forwarded by the authorities of Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't believe we do have that on our table. That's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It's -- the problem is this: That I think what happened is this. If you look at the English version, you will see first line illegible. If you look at the B/C/S version, indeed, you have a first line illegible. However, if you go through the document, itself, I'm talking of P546, if you go through the document, say, for example, when you arrive at ERN number 03652131 it's no longer illegible. There you see that indeed the words [B/C/S spoken] and it's -- definitely there you have at the top of the page of each page in B/C/S a statement, "documents provided by Republika Srpska." It did not show up in all the pages -- in any of the pages of the translation, unfortunately, because it could have shown up, but it does show up then in P547. This is the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Following up from that, that's correct, isn't it, these are documents forwarded, prepared even, by the authorities of Republika Srpska and not documents which were found in Srebrenica in July 1995 at all. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: In addition to the documents seized by the VRS in Srebrenica, on the list of the documents and the documents forwarded by the authorities of Republika Srpska, a part of the documents not related to that portion of them can also be found. This report of the commissariat for refugees in Belgrade, delivered to the authorities of Republika Srpska, was then forwarded from Banja Luka to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing again, I mean, we have -- I mean, I fully understand why Mr. Jones is putting these questions to you, which are very much articulated, because this column here, Witness, this last column here, basically should indicate seizure, seizure details. I can understand a document being seized in Srebrenica in 1995 during or following the takeover, but if it is delivered by Don Perry for Major Ranko Todorovic, for example in document number 60, or Don King from Jovanovic on the Srebrenica -- in the Srebrenica police station, 108, that is understandable. But then when you find in 105 and 106, Deyan Mihovles from Les Amis Du Commissariat De Belgrade Les Refugies in 1996, that requires an explanation. Of course, while the others are indicative of that they were seized in Srebrenica and fell in the hands of one individual, another individual, another individual and somehow they were all subsequently channelled to the authorities of Republika Srpska, there is no indication here that these were seized in Srebrenica. I don't know. So that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, to make the point finally on this, P293, which is number 104, which Your Honour I believe listed just now, I think that would bear having a look at, so if the witness can be shown P293.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is another case which obviously evidently would require some kind of explanation. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Radojicic, would you agree that we see at the top Romanija-Birac CSB, and then report by Maksim Maksimovic, that's a document created by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: This is certainly a document drawn up by the Serbs, but from the explanation I gave a little while ago, it's clear, and I wish to repeat, that these were documents delivered by the government of Republika Srpska. They could not have been seized in Srebrenica. So apart from the seized documents, there were also some other documents originating from Serb sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That brings us back to your original question and I think you ought to be satisfied with the answer now, basically the witness is saying that you do not read this document as meaning that each and every document that is listed there was necessarily seized in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Precisely, yes, Your Honour, we've arrived there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At least we have one or two instances which is indicative that they were supplied to Republika Srpska or they were furnished by Republika Srpska to the Tribunal but they need not have been seized from Srebrenica in 1995. They could have originated from some other place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, and without wanting to extend the exercise, I wouldn't want to say that it's limited to one or two instances because there is also number 133 which is an Official Gazette of the Serb people. There may be other examples in this table. It was really that the witness accept that he is not testifying that every one of the 186 documents were seized in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you accept that, Mr. Radojicic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Certainly I accept it. When I see how these documents were obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Just a few final questions and I trust Your Honours will bear with me as to the subject matter, which I submit is relevant. Following operation Krivaja, it's correct isn't it that the VRS killed thousands of unarmed men in Srebrenica, massacred them in cold blood? You're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: I am aware of that, especially after the analysis published by the commission for Srebrenica established by the government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that's the same operation in which these documents were allegedly seized?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Some of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In which some of these documents were allegedly seized?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Can you be more specific in your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Operation Krijava was the document - Krivaja, my apologies, Krivaja - was the operation during which some of these documents were seized by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the document originating from military sources were seized during that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. My suggestion to you, if you care to comment on it, is that an army which is prepared to commit such terrible massacres wouldn't scruple to commit the much less serious crime of forgery in order to distract attention from those massacres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer that question, witness, please. MR. DI FAZIO: Objection, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or else rephrase your question. But not the way you put it, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me put it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: These documents you've told us were provided to -- sorry, were collected at one point by Major Ranko Todorovic because they concerned crimes committed against the Serb people. Is that true, firstly? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, the evidence has been that the documentation passed through the hands of -- of Todorovic, not that he collected them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. As well, incidentally also I refer the parties and the transcript line 15, 16, of page 50 where my interruption, saying don't answer that question, please, Witness, is presented as forming part of the witness's answer. So that needs to be corrected. Apart from that, I think Mr. Di Fazio's objection is a valid one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, let me put it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Many of these documents concern allegations of crimes committed against the Serb people, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Many of these documents which you've testified about concern allegations of crimes committed against the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADOJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
